c: Rachel

Rachel, Laban’s beautiful younger daughter, was Jacob’s favorite wife. He first met her as he arrived at Paddan-aram in Haran, when he helped her remove the stone from a well and watered her father’s sheep (
). Jacob agreed to work seven years for Laban in order to have Rachel as his wife, and the time seemed like only a few days because of his great love for her.
Laban deceptively required Jacob to marry Leah, his older, less attractive daughter, before finally giving him Rachel. Unlike Leah, Rachel was barren in the early years of her marriage to Jacob (
). She gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob in order to have children by her, and Dan and Naphtali were born (
). In time, Rachel conceived and bore Joseph (
), and soon after, Jacob took his wives, children, and possessions away from Haran.
Somewhere between Bethel and Bethlehem, Rachel died while giving birth to Benjamin (
). Jacob set up a pillar over her tomb that was a landmark even in Saul’s time (
). Rachel and Leah are highly regarded for having built up the house of Israel (
). In

, Rachel is pictured as crying for her children being carried off into captivity, and Matthew recalls Jeremiah’s words at Herod’s slaughter of the male infants around Bethlehem shortly after Jesus’ birth (
Passages for Further Study
Leah
Leah was Laban’s first daughter, Jacob’s unloved first wife, and Rachel’s older sister.
After Jacob deceived his father Isaac into giving him the blessing intended for Esau (
), Jacob went to his uncle Laban in Mesopotamia to escape Esau’s revenge and find a wife (
). He fell in love with his cousin Rachel and arranged with her father to marry her after seven years of work (
). After the wedding feast, Laban deceived Jacob by giving him Leah instead of Rachel (
), claiming that custom required the older daughter to marry first (
). Leah was less attractive than her sister (
), and Jacob did not love her (

Jacob’s love for Rachel induced him to work another seven years to marry her. Because Jacob favored Rachel, the Lord blessed Leah with six sons and a daughter (Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah) before Rachel was able to conceive (
). At one point Rachel bargained with Leah for some mandrakes, a plant believed to ensure conception, in exchange for conjugal rights. Leah then conceived and bore her fifth son (
), increasing her advantage in her rivalry with Rachel.

Leah was the mother of two tribes that played particularly significant roles in Israelite history. The tribe of Levi was the tribe of the priesthood, and the tribe of Judah became the tribe of royalty through which the promised seed (
) came in the person of Jesus Christ.
Passages for Further Study

These chapters tell how God kept his promise by abundantly blessing Jacob with family and possessions. God also disciplined Jacob, leaving him to struggle with Laban for many years. Laban was Jacob’s match in deception, and thus a means of correction. • The story of Jacob and Laban parallels Israel’s later sojourn in Egypt. Jacob struggled while serving his uncle but finally emerged with a large family (the founders of the twelve tribes) and great wealth. In Egypt, the Israelites suffered under their oppressors, but they also flourished, becoming a great nation of twelve large tribes and escaping with great riches.

The rivalry between these sisters explains much of the later rivalry among their sons, and then among the tribes, just as the rivalry between Jacob and Laban foreshadowed conflict between Israel and the Arameans of Damascus (

). • God champions the cause of the poor and oppressed; he exalted Leah, the despised first wife, as the first to become a mother. Judah’s kingly tribe and Levi’s priestly line came through her despite Jacob’s favoritism for Rachel and her children. Despite the tension and jealousy resulting from Laban’s treachery and Jacob’s favoritism, God still built Jacob’s family and brought about the births of the tribal ancestors.

Rachel’s naming of sons through Bilhah does not reflect faith as Leah’s namings had. Rachel felt wronged over the marriage and her barrenness. The names of Bilhah’s sons reflect Rachel’s bitter struggle with her sister and her feeling of some victory.

After his fourteen years of service, Jacob asked Laban for permission to go home. The two bedouin leaders negotiated politely but remained cautiously on guard. Laban wanted to get more out of Jacob. Jacob wanted to gain his wages by selective breeding.
I have become wealthy:
God had prospered Laban through Jacob’s presence (see
). Laban may have looked for omens, or simply have perceived what was happening. Since dark-colored sheep (
) were rare, a large number of them was considered an omen of God’s blessing.

Jacob agreed that God had blessed Laban through him, so he made a plan to gain something for himself. He proposed for his wages the rare black and multicolored goats and the speckled and spotted sheep that were born.
As Abraham had done with Lot (
), Jacob gave Laban what he valued most. White sheep were more common and more valuable than dark or multicolored sheep; as a man of faith, Jacob was willing to take the rejects (cp.
Laban

Not to be outwitted, Jacob used selective breeding to acquire a flock, following the traditional belief that peeled sticks influenced the kind of animal that would be born.
